chunks: Some of the Mujabbirah, some from among the Mu'tazilah, and a man from the Zaydiyyah, in...
The gathering of al-Sharif Ahmad ibn al-Qasim al-'Alawi al-Muhammadi.

The shaykhs of the 'Abbasids and others. All of this is in addition to his discourse with many of the sects that existed at that time, such as the group of the Mu'tazilah, the people of doctrines, the theologians of the Mujabbirah, the Hashawiyyah, the Nasibiyyah, the Kaysaniyyah, the Isma'iliyyah, the Qaramitah, the Mubarakiyyah, the Nawusiyyah, the Shamtiyyah, the Fathiyyah, the Waqifah, and the Bashariyyah. This is what the reader comes upon in the sections from al-'Uyun and al-Mahasin mentioned above; so how would it be if one were to investigate the rest of his books and what was transmitted from him. It is noted that, sanctified be his secret, even during his travels he never ceased debating, calling to his principle, and defending his school. To demonstrate that, here is his conversation with a Zaydi man who wanted to defame him and bring him down, since his presence weighed heavily upon him and those like him, because wherever he settled, people gathered around him to benefit from him and receive from him. It happened that he once visited the sacred 'Alawi shrine and passed by the Mosque of Kufah, where more than five hundred people from its inhabitants and others gathered around him. A Zaydi man came forward, intending discord and defamation, and said to him: 'By what right did you permit yourself to deny the Imamate of Zayd?!' The Shaykh said to him: 'You have held a false assumption about me, and my statement concerning Zayd is one in which no one from the Zaydiyyah disagrees with me. Zayd, may Allah have mercy on him, was an Imam in knowledge, zuhd, enjoining good, and forbidding evil. What I deny of him is the Imamate that necessitates for its possessor 'ismah, explicit designation, and miracle. And on this no one from the Zaydiyyah disagrees with me.' None of those present from the Zaydiyyah could refrain from thanking him and praying for him, and the man's stratagem in what he intended of defamation and discord was nullified. In any case, the rank of this great scholar is too evident to require explanation, for tongues proclaimed in his name praise and commendation, and his merit became so well known that it rendered unnecessary extended mention of him and elaboration on his life. His virtue, knowledge, nobility, and glory furnish true testimonies to the loftiness of his station and the greatness of his genius, so much so that leading authorities spoke of that, thanking him for his benefactions, as he was a refuge for learners, a stronghold for scholars, a sanctuary for rulers, and a resort for the common people and everyone else. Brilliant fuqaha' sought him out and benefited from the spring of his knowledge, and master theologians came to him and sipped from his pure source. Even rulers and ministers would learn from him and depart fully watered from his stream. Thus Taj al-Millah wa 'Adud al-Dawlah Abu Shuja' 'Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Daylami learned fiqh from him, and despite his grandeur and power, he would visit him with his procession in his house and attend him when he was ill, in addition to his standing with the kings of the regions. Perhaps the encomiums of his biographers and the signs of praise for him spare us from lengthening the explanation of that, for the biographical dictionaries agree that he was: 'the Imam of the Rafidah, the shaykh of the Imamiyyah and its scholar, the defender of their domain, the author for them, the chief of kalam, fiqh, and disputation, foremost in the craft of fiqh and kalam, subtle in intelligence, ready in reply, sharp in mind, eloquent in speech and debate, patient with the opponent, beautiful in outward conduct, abundant in charity, immense in humility, frequent in salat and sawm, an ascetic worshipper; he debated the people of every creed, and he possessed force together with immense majesty in the Buyid state.' Thus do the dictionaries commend him and the biographers praise him, among whom were some of his contemporaries from hostile enemies and obstinate envier-opponents who were distressed by him, and whose patience wore thin because of his long life among them; so they wished for his death due to the intensity of their envy and their inability to attain his rank or contend with him in procession or stature. They envied the youth when they could not reach his striving; so the people are enemies to him and adversaries. It is sufficient proof of the loftiness of his rank and the greatness of his majesty that he was the one looked to within the Imamiyyah and the one sought from among them in every difficult problem and issue.

Thus he would suffer some harm from the disturbances of the common people and the ignorant masses, and many of his opponents—those who had not reached his stature nor attained his striving—would exploit events during the outbreaks that used to arise in Baghdad between the Shi'ah and the Sunnah, inciting them against him and urging them on against him. Among that was that in the year 398, some low people from Bab al-Basrah targeted the Shaykh in his mosque in al-Karkh at Darb Rabah, harmed him, and reviled him. The Shaykh's companions rose in anger over this, called one another out, and went to the house of al-Qadi Abu Muhammad Ibn al-Akfani and Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini, insulting the two of them and seeking the fuqaha' among their followers in order to attack them, but they fled, and Abu Hamid moved to Dar al-Qatan. The turmoil grew severe, and news of it reached the caliph, who became angry and sent his aides to support Ahl al-Sunnah. They burned many of the houses of the Shi'ah, seized a group of them and imprisoned them, and sent 'Amid al-Juyush to exile the Shaykh from Baghdad because he was the faqih of the Shi'ah, as revenge for Abu Hamid and his group. So the Shaykh was expelled from Baghdad, then 'Ali ibn Mazid interceded for him and he was returned to it. The Shaykh was also among those who signed the document that contained disparagement of the lineage of the 'Alawis in Egypt, as Ibn al-Athir mentioned in his al-Kamil. He wrote in the year 403 a document in which, among the 'Alawis, al-Murtada, al-Radi, Ibn al-Bathawi al-'Alawi, Ibn al-Azraq al-Musawi, and al-Zaki Abu Ya'la 'Umar ibn Muhammad signed; and among the judges and scholars there signed Ibn al-Akfani, Ibn al-Kharzi, Abu al-'Abbas al-Abyurdi, Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini, Abu 'Abd Allah ibn al-Nu'man, the faqih of the Shi'ah, al-Kashfali, al-Qaduri, al-Saymari, Ibn al-Baydawi, al-Nasawi, and others.

key_terms.الزَّيْدِيَّةِ: the Zaydi sect, mentioned in connection with debate over the Imamate of Zayd
key_terms.النَّصَّ: explicit designation, a defining proof for the rightful Imam
key_terms.الْإِمَامَةَ: Imamate, here referring specifically to the doctrinal leadership entailing special qualifications
key_terms.الْعِصْمَةَ: 'ismah, the infallibility associated with the Imam in Imamiyyah doctrine
key_terms.الْفِتْنَةُ: civil strife or sectarian turmoil, especially in the events of Baghdad
key_terms.الْفِقْهِ: fiqh, Islamic jurisprudence, one of the sciences in which the scholar excelled
key_terms.الْمُعْجِزَ: miracle, cited as one of the marks linked to the doctrinal Imamate
key_terms.الْمُنَاظَرَةِ: scholarly disputation or debate with opposing sects and thinkers

ai.seo_question: What does this biographical report reveal about the scholarly status, debates, and public trials of a major Imamiyyah scholar in Baghdad?
ai.summary: This passage is a biographical account highlighting the scholarly stature, theological debates, and social influence of a prominent Imamiyyah scholar. It records his engagement with various sects, his clarification regarding Zayd's status, and the political and sectarian tensions he faced in Baghdad.
